About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Computer Science Years 12–13 of
the New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Computer Science Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Computer Science Years 12–13 is proposed to
be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Computer Science Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12
from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Through the study of Years 12–13 Computer Science students are taught to apply
computational thinking, manage and analyse data, design and develop software, and
evaluate digital solutions. They learn to formulate problems, create and refine
algorithms and programs, represent and manage data, and evaluate digital systems
in terms of efficiency, reliability, security, and usability. Students also examine the
broader implications of digital systems and emerging technologies, including privacy,
cybersecurity, bias, data sovereignty, and the responsible use of emerging
technologies.

Years 12–13 Computer Science provides students with the knowledge and practices
to investigate problems, design digital solutions, and evaluate the effectiveness of
computational approaches. Through iterative processes of analysis, design,
development, testing, and evaluation, students learn to apply computational thinking,
data management, software development, and artificial intelligence (AI) concepts to
real-world contexts. They develop an understanding of how digital systems are
designed, implemented, and refined to meet user needs, while considering technical,
ethical, cultural, and societal factors.

As students progress through Years 12–13 Computer Science, they extend their
understanding of algorithms, data systems, software development, and AI. They learn
to evaluate the efficiency, scalability, reliability, and security of digital systems; apply
advanced programming and design practices; and analyse the opportunities and
challenges associated with emerging technologies. Through this process, students

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within Computer Science.
 In Computer Science, writing is an analytical and reflective practice that enables students to communicate informed understandings of how digital systems work.

All knowledge and practices are compulsory. However, schools can determine how
learning is organised across the year, including integrating content from multiple
elements and strands where this supports coherence and depth. Examples are
provided as guidance only; as long as the intended knowledge and practices are met,
schools and teachers may substitute contexts and examples that better reflect local
environments, iwi and hapū connections, student interests, and teacher expertise.

Disciplinary writing is included in the teaching sequence to set out what subject-
specific literacy is to be taught. It is organised into a knowledge component that is
consistent across all year levels and a practice component sequenced across years.
